question: A 2 Ω resistance is connected to a 4 Ω resistance in series. Their equivalent resistance will be:
solution:
The correct answer is __**6 Ω**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• For resistors in series, **equivalent resistance adds directly**: **Rₑq = R₁ + R₂**.
 
• Substituting the values: **Rₑq = 2 Ω + 4 Ω =** **6 Ω**.
 
• In a series circuit, the **same current** flows through each resistor, so adding resistance increases total opposition to current.
 
• The result **6 Ω corresponds to Option 3**, which is larger than each individual resistance, as expected for series connections.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Resistance (R)**

 
 
• Measures how strongly a component opposes electric current.
 
• Unit is the **ohm** denoted by the Greek letter **Ω**.
 
• Depends on material resistivity, length, and cross-sectional area of the conductor.
 
• Measured using an ohmmeter or via V and I using Ohm’s law.
 
 
 
• **Series Connection**
 
 
• Components are connected end to end, forming a single path for current.
 
• **Current is the same** through all elements; voltages divide across them.
 
• Total or equivalent resistance is the **sum** of individual resistances.
 
• Characteristic check: Rₑq is always **greater than** any individual series resistor.
 
 
 
• **Equivalent Resistance**
 
 
• A single resistance that can replace a combination with the same V–I behavior at its terminals.
 
• For series: **Rₑq = R₁ + R₂ + R₃ + …**
 
• Contrast with parallel: **1/Rₑq = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂ + …**, where Rₑq is less than the smallest branch.
 
• Useful for simplifying networks before applying circuit laws.
 
 
 
• **Ohm’s Law and Voltage Drops**
 
 
• Ohm’s law: **V = I R**, relates voltage, current, and resistance.
 
• In series, with current I, each drop is **Vₖ = I Rₖ**; the source voltage equals the sum of drops.
 
• Example check: if a 12 V source drives 2 Ω and 4 Ω in series, Rₑq = 6 Ω, so I = 12/6 = 2 A; drops are 4 V and 8 V.
 
• This verifies both the arithmetic and the distribution of voltages in series circuits.
 
 
 
• **Power Considerations**
 
 
• Power dissipated: **P = I²R = V²/R = V I**.
 
• In series, the higher resistance **dissipates more power** for the same current.
 
• For the example above at 2 A: P₂Ω = 8 W, P₄Ω = 16 W, total 24 W equals source power.
 
• Ensures component ratings are not exceeded during operation.
